opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely encouraging, but I'm cautious about calling it progress on energy use without some caveats.

On the positive side, it's a real shift in mindset. For a few years the dominant narrative was that bigger is always better: more parameters, more data, more compute. Now we're seeing a lot of work showing that a well-trained smaller model, or a distilled or quantized one, can do as well or nearly as well on many tasks. Per query, that can mean a meaningful drop in energy, and it means people can run models on more modest hardware, sometimes even locally, which is good for access too.

But I always come back to two things. The first is rebound, or Jevons paradox. When something becomes cheaper and more efficient to use, we tend to use a lot more of it. If smaller models make it trivial to put generative AI into every app, every search, every email client, total energy consumption can still go up even if each individual inference is more efficient. So efficiency per model doesn't automatically translate into lower overall impact.

The second is that "small" is relative and often hides where the costs actually are. A lot of these smaller models are distilled from very large ones, so the energy cost of training that big teacher model is still part of the story. And there's the question of what task you're using it for. A model with a few billion parameters is small compared to the frontier models, but if you're using it for something a simple classifier could handle, you're still using far more energy than you need to. In our work comparing models across tasks, the biggest differences often come from the type of task, generative versus discriminative, and from choosing a general-purpose model where a task-specific one would do.

So what I'd like to see is less "small models will save us" and more transparency and measurement. We need standardized ways of reporting energy for both training and inference, so that developers and users can actually compare options and make informed choices. Without that, efficiency gains are a bit of a black box: we hope they're happening, but we can't really verify the net effect. Smaller models are a step in the right direction, but only if we pair them with sober choices about when and how much we deploy AI in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says energy reporting lacks transparency and standardization, making it hard to compare options or verify the net effect.

r002.rationale: It explains that per-query efficiency may not lower total energy because use can expand, large teacher models still carry training costs, and the net effect remains unverified.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So I think it's genuinely a positive trend, but I want to be careful about what we mean by "progress," because there are a few things going on at once.

On the technical side, yes, a smaller model that does the same task uses less energy per inference. That's just arithmetic. When we've done measurements on Hugging Face, running a model that's a few hundred million parameters versus one that's tens of billions, you're talking about orders of magnitude difference in energy per query. And I think the more interesting thing is that for a lot of real-world tasks, classification, extraction, summarization of a specific kind of document, the small model is just as good. People reach for the giant general-purpose model out of habit, or because it's the thing with the API, not because the task requires it. So the trend toward smaller, task-specific models is really a trend toward right-sizing, and I'm very much in favor of that.

But here's where I get more cautious. First, efficiency gains at the model level don't automatically translate into efficiency gains at the system level. This is the Jevons paradox, which I end up bringing up on basically every podcast I do. If you make something cheaper and faster to run, people run it more. We saw this with DeepSeek, right? There was all this excitement that a model was trained for a fraction of the compute, and the stock market panicked for about a day, and then everyone said "great, now we can deploy this everywhere." Smaller and cheaper per query often means more queries, more features with AI bolted on, more agents running in the background that nobody asked for. So the total footprint can go up even as the per-unit cost goes down.

Second, a lot of the small models we're excited about are distilled from very large models. So the training cost of the big model is still in there, it's just amortized or hidden. You can't really claim the small model is efficient without accounting for what it took to make it possible.

And third, and this is maybe the thing I care most about, we still can't measure this properly. The companies deploying the biggest models don't disclose energy per query, don't disclose what hardware it runs on, don't disclose the carbon intensity of their grids. So when someone says "our new model is more efficient," I have no way to verify that. It's a claim, not a measurement. That's actually why we've been pushing for things like an energy score, something like the Energy Star rating for appliances, so that a developer choosing between models can actually see the numbers side by side.

So my assessment is: smaller models are necessary for progress on energy, but they're not sufficient. The progress comes when efficiency is paired with transparency and with some restraint about where AI gets deployed in the first place. If we just use efficiency as permission to put a language model behind every button in every app, we haven't actually solved anything, we've just made the problem harder to see.

r001.rationale: The response says companies do not disclose energy use, hardware, or grid carbon intensity, making efficiency claims impossible to verify.

r002.rationale: It explains that efficiency gains can increase total use, and that small models may carry hidden training costs from the larger models they were distilled from; it concludes that smaller models are necessary but insufficient for energy progress.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between efficiency and total energy use. A smaller model might use less energy for a given task, and that’s progress. But if it becomes cheaper and easier to deploy, and we end up using it a hundred times more, the total energy consumption can still go up. That’s the rebound effect.

So I’d want to know: compared to what, doing which task, and at what scale? Are we replacing a larger model with a smaller one that does the job just as well, or are we adding AI to applications that didn’t need it before? You also have to look beyond training to the energy used every time people interact with the model.

Smaller models are a promising direction, but model size alone doesn’t tell us whether we’re reducing energy use. We need measurements of actual deployment and total consumption to make that claim.

r001.rationale: The response calls for measurements of actual deployment and total consumption, but does not identify limited transparency as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: The response says smaller models alone do not prove reduced energy use, citing increased usage and rebound effects. It does not communicate that smaller models being developed alongside larger models is not a clear energy win.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between efficiency and total energy use. A smaller model might use less energy for a particular task, and that’s useful progress, especially if it can do that task just as well. But if we then deploy it in ten times as many places, the total energy consumption can still go up. That’s the rebound effect: making something cheaper and more efficient can encourage us to use more of it.

So I’d want to know: more efficient compared to what, for which task, and at what scale? We need to measure the energy used in deployment, as well as training, and look at absolute consumption. Smaller models are a promising direction, but their size alone doesn’t tell us whether we’re reducing our overall environmental impact.

r001.rationale: The response calls for measuring energy use but does not identify limited transparency as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says efficiency gains may be offset by increased deployment, but does not address smaller models being developed alongside larger models.
